name: Grecian Rose
lede: Grecian Rose is a dusty, dark yellowish pink first recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1927, sitting so close to Orange-Vinaceous and Peach Rose in color space that the three names mark almost the same shade.

sections.title: A pink by another name
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives Grecian Rose at plate 3 F 9, first recorded in 1927 [1]. The same plate carries two later variants at almost the same spot: Moss Rose, recorded in 1892, and Starflower, recorded in 1928 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 would call this a light grayish red, a salmon tone warmed by a touch of brown [2].

The nearest named colors are [[peach-rose|Peach Rose]], 2.7 units away and almost the same shade read under a different name, and [[new-york-pink|New York Pink]], 3.2 units away [2]. "Grecian" borrows classical-world prestige the way many early-twentieth-century paint and fabric names did; no source consulted explains the choice beyond that [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Grecian Rose appears in 83 of our 23,781 paintings, as photographed, rarer than 60 percent of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 6 of 1,674 paintings, at 2.6 times the expected rate for that century [3]. Where it appears, it most often plays an accent rather than a base tone [3]. The earliest match is dated 1301, 629 years before Maerz and Paul's 1927 record — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that the same dye or pigment made it, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

origin.named_after: undocumented; "Grecian" is a decorative, not etymological, label
origin.source: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color (1930), plate 3 F 9

questions.q: Which dictionary first records Grecian Rose, in 1927?
True or false: Grecian Rose is a clearly distinct shade from its nearest named neighbors.

openers: Grecian Rose sits so close to two other names that only 2.7 units of color space separate them.

issues: Fixed: the lede said Grecian Rose, Orange-Vinaceous and Peach Rose 'mark almost the same point on the page' — but Orange-Vinaceous and Peach Rose come from Ridgway (1912), not from Maerz and Paul's plate 3 (where Grecian Rose, Moss Rose and Starflower actually sit together); the three colors are close only by computed color distance, not by any shared page. Reworded to 'in color space ... almost the same shade.'
